one_sentence_story: Rosenhan's 1973 hospital study showed how a sticky diagnostic label could make staff chart normal notebook-writing as 'writing behavior' — while modern archival sleuthing revealed Rosenhan's own paper cut corners too, teaching a double lesson in confirmation bias and open data.
so_what_for_you: Separate raw behavior from the sticky label on top of the folder: evaluate what someone actually did today before filtering every ordinary habit through last year's reputation.

jargon_map.plain: once an authoritative label is applied, reinterpreting every normal action to fit that label
jargon_map.analogy: like assuming every cough from someone who once smoked is lung disease

jargon_map.plain: describing ordinary boredom, waiting for lunch, or taking notes in clinical jargon
jargon_map.analogy: like calling reading before bed 'nocturnal text fixation'

jargon_map.plain: doctors erring toward admitting healthy people to avoid missing one sick patient, versus doubting real patients in Study 2
jargon_map.analogy: like a smoke alarm tuned ultra-sensitive vs unplugged

jargon_map.plain: explicit, reproducible symptom-and-duration rules introduced in DSM-III after 1973
jargon_map.analogy: like using a calibrated thermometer instead of guessing fever by touch
